'''John Matthew Martinis''' (born 1958)  is an American [[physicist]] and Professor of Physics at the [[University of California, Santa Barbara]].<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |title=John M. Martinis |url=https://www.ucsb.edu/about/faculty-and-alumni/john-martinis |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251010142952/http://www.ucsb.edu/about/faculty-and-alumni/john-martinis |archive-date=2025-10-10 |access-date=2025-10-10 |website=UC Santa Barbara |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://thedailyguardian.com/world/us/who-is-john-m-martinis-nobel-prize-in-physics-2025-winners-education-other-awards-669169/ |title=Who is John M. Martinis? Nobel Prize in Physics 2025 Winner's Education & Other Awards |website=The Daily Guardian |date= October 7, 2025|access-date= October 7, 2025}}</ref> He led a team to develop a [[superconducting quantum computer]] at the [[Quantum AI Lab]]. With the [[Sycamore processor]], the team claimed the first evidence of [[quantum supremacy]] in 2019. He shared the 2025 [[Nobel Prize in Physics]] with [[John Clarke (physicist)|John Clarke]] and [[Michel Devoret]] for joint work on [[macroscopic quantum phenomena]] in [[Superconductivity|superconductors]].<ref name=":0" />

== Early life and education ==
John Matthew Martinis was born in 1958 and raised in [[San Pedro, Los Angeles]].<ref name=":3">{{Cite news |date=October 7, 2025 |title=2025 Nobel Prize Resources – Meet the Laureates |url=https://www.aip.org/nobel-prize |access-date=October 7, 2025 |work=AIP.ORG |issn=}}</ref> His father, a [[Croat]] from [[Komiža]] on the island of [[Vis (island)|Vis]] near [[Split, Croatia|Split]], Croatia,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Dimitropoulos |first=George |date=10 October 2025 |title=New generation will make the quantum revolution a reality,' says Nobel laureate John Martinis |url=https://www.euronews.com/next/2025/10/10/new-generation-will-make-the-quantum-revolution-a-reality-says-nobel-laureate-john-martini |access-date=2025-10-13 |website=Euronews}}</ref> immigrated to the United States from Yugoslavia to escape [[Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia|the communist regime]].<ref name=":3"/> His mother was born in San Pedro to parents who had also emigrated from Croatia.<ref>{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aXzkY8-cxoI |title=Ekskluzivan intervju s dobitnikom Nobelove nagrade Johnom Martinisom |date=2025-12-19 |last=Glas Hrvatske {{!}} HRT |access-date=2026-01-03 |via=YouTube}}</ref>

Martinis studied physics at the [[University of California, Berkeley]], where he received a [[Bachelor of Science]] in 1980 and a [[Doctor of Philosophy]] in 1987.<ref>{{Cite news |date=October 7, 2025 |title=Meet the 2025 Nobel prize winners in Physics: Where they studied and how their research shaped quantum science |url=https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/education/news/meet-the-nobel-2025-laureates-in-physics-where-they-studied-and-how-their-research-shaped-quantum-science/articleshow/124361344.cms |access-date=October 7, 2025 |work=The Times of India |issn=0971-8257}}</ref>

During his doctoral studies, Martinis investigated the quantum behaviour of a macroscopic variable, the phase difference across a [[Josephson effect|Josephson tunnel junction]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Clarke|first1=J.|last2=Cleland|first2=A. N.|last3=Devoret|first3=M. H.|last4=Esteve|first4=D.|last5=Martinis|first5=J. M.|date=February 26, 1988|title=Quantum mechanics of a macroscopic variable: the phase difference of a josephson junction|journal=Science|volume=239|issue=4843|pages=992–997|doi=10.1126/science.239.4843.992|issn=0036-8075|pmid=17815701|bibcode=1988Sci...239..992C |s2cid=1732678}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Hassinger |first=Sebastian |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cE8hEQAAQBAJ&dq=martinis+phd+%22advisor%22+clarke+devoret&pg=PA113 |title=The New Quantum Era |date=September 11, 2024 |publisher=O'Reilly Media, Inc. |isbn=978-1-0981-4938-3 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite thesis|last=Martinis|first=J. M.|year=1985|title=Macroscopic Quantum Tunneling and Energy-Level Quantization in the Zero Voltage State of the Current-Biased Josephson Junction|url=https://escholarship.org/uc/item/5kr3d1ff|degree=Ph.D.|id={{Proquest|303359571}}}}</ref> His doctoral advisor was [[John Clarke (physicist)|John Clarke]].<ref name=":1" /> During this time, he collaborated with [[Michel Devoret]], a [[postdoctoral researcher]] at the time.<ref name=":1" />[[File:Prospects for a Quantum Factoring Machine.webm|thumb|thumbtime=0:58|Martinis giving a lecture in 2017]]In 1985, Clarke, Devoret, and Martinis presented their analysis of microwave pulses that demonstrated the [[Phase qubit#Quantized energy levels|quantized energy levels]] of a [[Josephson junction]].<ref name=":1" /> This work would later become the basis for [[superconducting quantum computing]].<ref name=":1" />

On September 21, 2026, the Prime Minister of Croatia, [[Andrej Plenković]], granted Martinis Croatian citizenship.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Plenković Nobelovcu hrvatskih korijena svečano dodijelio domovnicu |url=https://vijesti.hrt.hr/svijet/un-6-12917878 |access-date=September 21, 2026 |website=[[Croatian Radiotelevision|HRT]] |date=September 21, 2026 |language=hr}}</ref>

== Career ==
Martinis joined the [[CEA Paris-Saclay]] in France<ref name=":2" /> for a first postdoc, and then the Electromagnetic Technology division at the [[National Institute of Standards and Technology]] (NIST) in Boulder, where he worked on [[SQUID|superconducting quantum interference device]] (SQUIDs) amplifiers.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Welty|first1=Richard P.|last2=Martinis|first2=John M.|date=March 1993|title=Two-stage integrated SQUID amplifier with series array output|url=https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/1993ITAS....3.2605W/abstract|journal=IEEE Transactions on Applied Superconductivity|volume=3|issue=1 |pages=2605–2608|doi=10.1109/77.233523|bibcode=1993ITAS....3.2605W |s2cid=33500389|issn=1051-8223}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last=Rogers |first=Kara |date=October 7, 2025 |title=John M. Martinis |url=https://www.britannica.com/biography/John-M-Martinis |access-date=October 8, 2025 |website=www.britannica.com |language=en}}</ref>

Since 2004, Martinis has served on the faculty of the [[University of California, Santa Barbara]].<ref name=":4" /> He held the title of Susan and Bruce Worster Chair in Experimental Physics for many years. The quantum device he developed in collaboration with UCSB colleagues was named [[Science (journal)|''Science'' magazine's]] 2010 Breakthrough of the Year.<ref name=":4" /> [[Quantum Artificial Intelligence Lab|Google Quantum AI Lab]], a partnership between UC Santa Barbara and Google, announced in 2014 that it had hired Martinis and his team in a multimillion dollar deal to build a [[quantum computing|quantum computer]] using superconducting [[Qubit|qubits]].<ref name="forbes2020">{{Cite web |date=April 30, 2020 |title=Google's Top Quantum Scientist Explains In Detail Why He Resigned |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/moorinsights/2020/04/30/googles-top-quantum-scientist-explains-in-detail-why-he-resigned/ |access-date=January 18, 2025 |work=forbes.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Finley |first=Klint |date=September 5, 2014 |title=The Man Who Will Build Google's Elusive Quantum Computer |url=https://www.wired.com/2014/09/martinis/ |access-date=November 2, 2019 |magazine=Wired |issn=1059-1028}}</ref> He and his team published a paper in ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'' in 2019,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Arute|first1=Frank|last2=Arya|first2=Kunal|last3=Babbush|first3=Ryan|last4=Bacon|first4=Dave|last5=Bardin|first5=Joseph C.|last6=Barends|first6=Rami|last7=Biswas|first7=Rupak|last8=Boixo|first8=Sergio|last9=Brandao|first9=Fernando G. S. L.|last10=Buell|first10=David A.|last11=Burkett|first11=Brian|date=October 2019|title=Quantum supremacy using a programmable superconducting processor|journal=Nature|volume=574|issue=7779|pages=505–510|doi=10.1038/s41586-019-1666-5 | arxiv=1910.11333 |pmid=31645734|bibcode=2019Natur.574..505A |issn=1476-4687|doi-access=free}}</ref> where they presented how they achieved [[quantum supremacy]] for the first time using the [[Sycamore processor]], a 53-qubit quantum processor.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.scottaaronson.com/blog/?p=4372|title=Shtetl-Optimized » Blog Archive » Quantum supremacy: the gloves are off|date=October 23, 2019 |access-date=November 4, 2019}}</ref> Martinis resigned from Google in April 2020 after being reassigned to an advisory role.<ref>{{Cite magazine|url=https://www.wired.com/story/googles-head-quantum-computing-hardware-resigns/|title=Google's Head of Quantum Computing Hardware Resigns|magazine=Wired|access-date=April 21, 2020|language=en|issn=1059-1028}}</ref><ref name="forbes2020" />

In 2020, Martinis joined [[Silicon Quantum Computing]], a start-up founded in Australia by Professor [[Michelle Simmons]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=September 29, 2020 |title=Ex-Google quantum chief joins Simmons' silicon startup |url=https://www.innovationaus.com/ex-google-quantum-chief-joins-simmons-silicon-startup/ |access-date=September 29, 2020 |website=InnovationAus |language=en-US}}</ref>

In 2026, he was appointed to the [[President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology]] (PCAST) by President [[Donald Trump]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=President Trump Announces Appointments to President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology |url=https://www.whitehouse.gov/articles/2026/03/president-trump-announces-appointments-to-presidents-council-of-advisors-on-science-and-technology/ |date=March 25, 2026 |access-date=March 26, 2026 |publisher=[[The White House]]}}</ref>

===Qolab===
In 2022, together with CEO Alan Ho, he founded Qolab, a quantum computing private company based on semiconductor chip manufacturing.<ref>{{Cite web |date=October 9, 2025 |title=California physicist and Nobel laureate John Martinis won't quit on quantum computers |url=https://www.latimes.com/science/story/2025-10-09/california-physicist-wins-nobel-prize |access-date=October 10, 2025 |website=Los Angeles Times |language=en-US}}</ref>

Since 2025, Qolab and Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) are co-leading a consortium for the [[DARPA]] Quantum Benchmarking Initiative (QBI). The team is tasked with building an industrially useful quantum supercomputer by 2033. Within this partnership, Martinis and Qolab lead the hardware build, designing and fabricating the core superconducting quantum processors.<ref>{{cite web |title=Qolab Spearheads Hardware Development for DARPA's Quantum Benchmarking Initiative |url=https://www.hpcwire.com/off-the-wire/qolab-spearheads-hardware-development-for-darpas-quantum-benchmarking-initiative/ |website=HPCwire |access-date=19 July 2026}}</ref><ref name="Quantum Insider">{{cite news |last1=Rehman |first1=Mohib Ur |title=Qolab Strengthens Position with Strategic Partnerships and Global Expansion in 2025 |url=https://thequantuminsider.com/2025/12/23/qolab-2025-strategic-collaborations/ |work=The Quantum Insider |date=23 December 2025}}</ref> In December 2025, Qolab launched Qolab Start, a superconducting qubit platform for hardware research and workforce development.<ref name="Quantum Insider"/> Built for universities, research labs, and workforce training, it eliminates the need to build custom labs by providing pre-packaged hardware and direct access to quantum processors. Researchers can access these systems via an on-premise installation or through the cloud.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Warfield |first1=Win |title=Qolab Raises $54.2M Led by UC Investments to Advance Quantum Processors |url=https://www.citybiz.co/article/872953/qolab-raises-54-2m-led-by-uc-investments-to-advance-quantum-processors/ |work=citybiz |date=13 July 2026}}</ref> In February 2026, Singapore's National Quantum Federated Foundry (NQFF) and Qolab formed a research collaboration to build integrated cryogenic low-pass filters (LPFs) for quantum processors.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Abdel-Kareem |first1=Mohamed |title=NQFF and Qolab Collaborate on Wafer-Scale Cryogenic Filters for Quantum Scaling |url=https://quantumcomputingreport.com/nqff-and-qolab-collaborate-on-wafer-scale-cryogenic-filters-for-quantum-scaling/ |work=Quantum Computing Report |date=23 February 2026}}</ref>
 
Martinis is the co-leader of Quantum Scaling Alliance (QSA), a global group that develops quantum computing technology and include Qolab as well as others such as [[Applied Materials]], HPE, Synopsys.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Marias |first1=Stephen Las |title=Nobel Laureate John Martinis Launches Quantum Manufacturing Alliance |url=https://www.eetasia.com/nobel-laureate-john-martinis-launches-quantum-manufacturing-alliance/ |work=EE Times Asia |date=29 December 2025 |language=en}}</ref>
